notes.text: Malayalam verbs never change for person. Njaan varunnu, avan varunnu, ningal varunnu: one form carries everyone.
Namaskaram is kept for guests and strangers. Friends skip it and open with entha visesham: what is the news?
Three words for you: nee for close friends, ningal for polite distance, thangal when respect really matters.
Kerala once passed property through mothers, so ammaavan, your mother's brother, still weighs more than any other uncle.
Rice changes its name as it travels: nellu in the field, ari in the sack, choru on your plate.
Zero is poojyam, literally the one worthy of worship. Even emptiness was given a respectful name here.
Pacha is green and also raw. Pacha vellam is plain water, and pachaykku parayuka means to speak bluntly.
Ask for the way using vazhi. And you never get off a bus, you irangunnu, you climb down.
English needs four words for the day after tomorrow. Malayalam says marunnaal, and mininnale for the day before yesterday.
Venam means I want it, venda means I do not. One syllable stands between buying and walking away.
Sugham holds health, comfort and ease together, so sugamaano asks after your whole state, not only your body.
Veedu is the house you live in. Tharavadu is the ancestral home a family still names itself after.
Pani means work, but pani kitti means you landed in trouble. Tone decides whether someone is busy or doomed.
Kothi has no English twin: that precise craving when somebody else's plate smells better than your own.
Onam follows Kerala's own calendar, in the month of Chingam, and neighbours of every faith wish each other Onaashamsakal.
